source: Public decision observations from seeded development simulations. Only the acting player cards and public state are retained. Review judgments are not solver-certified labels.

cases.review: A4 suited calls a five-bet to 67.5 BB, then calls off on K-J-T without a pair. An occasional A4s four-bet bluff is defensible; continuing this far needs a much stronger justification. Fold to the five-bet as the training default.

TT shoves over a turn raise on 6h 9d Jd Ac. This is an underpair with no flush draw or one-card straight draw. The raise represents a much stronger range than random cards; prefer folding to the raise in a basic value-oriented policy.

QT shoves over a river raise on 8c 3d 6d 2h Td. Top pair is a bluff-catcher on a completed flush board. Prefer folding to the raise unless a credible bluffing read supports calling; a value reraise needs worse callers.

KK raises an ace-river lead on Td 4d 6s 8c Ac, then calls a shove. The river devalues KK; raising mostly folds out worse hands and retains aces or better. Consider call or fold based on the betting range, rather than an automatic value raise.

77 raises on 9d 6d Ks 9s 3d and calls a reraise. The flush completed, and kings, nines and larger pocket pairs beat this hand. Fold to the reraise as a training default; the initial raise also lacks a clear value target.

A4 suited calls a river shove on 3c 8c 9s 9h 5h after missing clubs. Only the board pair and ace kicker play. Earlier three-betting and a flop raise make a random-hand equity baseline inappropriate. Prefer folding this river bluff-catcher without an explicit bluff-frequency read.

TT raises the flop bet and shoves over a turn lead on Ks 9h 3d Kc. This converts a hand with showdown value into an expensive raise without a defined bluff or value target. Calling or folding should be evaluated against the actual range; shoving is a poor automatic default.

A7 shoves over a river three-bet on Tc Kh 2s Ks Ah. It has aces and kings with a ten kicker; the seven does not play. Any king, AQ, AJ or QJ beats it; AT ties it. Prefer folding to this reraise in the basic training policy.

66 check-raises and then calls a large river reraise on 5h 9h 2c 2d Qc. The pocket pair is below both queen and nine, and trips or better are plausible. Prefer folding to the reraise; the check-raise also needs a defensible bluff rationale.

K8 suited calls a turn check-raise and river shove on 8c 9h 9c 4s 5c. Its effective holding is a pair of eights with the board pair, and clubs complete. Prefer folding by the river unless the opponent is known to overbluff this line.

A3 offsuit calls from the small blind, continues versus a squeeze, then calls 11 BB on 6h 9h 7s with no pair, heart, or one-card straight draw. This is too weak as a standard training continuation versus a three-bettor. Fold preflop or on the flop.

TT shoves over a third barrel on Ac 3s 6s 8s 5h. The Ts blocker can matter for a deliberately constructed bluff, but the current policy uses generic value equity rather than such a plan. Prefer folding this bluff-catcher as the training default.

A3 shoves over a river raise on 5d 5c Kc 4s Kd. It is playing kings and fives with an ace kicker; any king or five beats it. This is a bluff-catcher, not an automatic value reraise. Prefer folding to the raise without a specific exploit.

K9 offsuit calls a button limp-reraise from the small blind. It is out of position and easily dominated by a normal three-betting range. Fold as the default. Dev wins this particular hand, which does not validate the preflop call.
AT shoves over a river check-raise on 6h Ts Jc 6s 9c. This is tens and sixes, below any jack, six, overpair or completed straight. Prefer folding to the check-raise in the basic policy.

A9 shoves over a river raise on Kd 4h 8d 2h Ad. Top pair with a nine kicker is a bluff-catcher against this line, and diamonds completed. Prefer folding to the raise as a training default; a call requires a bluff-frequency case.
K3 shoves over a river raise on 6s As 4c 8s Kc. It has second pair with a weak kicker on a three-spade board. Prefer folding to the raise; the shove has no clear value target.
QJ shoves over a river lead on 8c 9h Jh 6s Ad. The ace turns top pair into second pair on a connected board. Call or fold needs range analysis; automatically raising for value is suspect.

96 raises and calls a shove on Qs 6s Tc Jh Th. It has tens and sixes, losing to any queen, jack, ten and many straights. Prefer folding to the shove; the first raise also needs a clear bluff rationale.

K9 offsuit four-bets a 25-BB big blind to 22.5 BB. This nearly commits the opponent while using a hand often dominated when continued against. Prefer folding to the three-bet. The later 2.5-BB call is cheap and is not the main mistake.

K9 repeatedly reraises on Kc 7d 6c 5h 6s, turning a 2-BB limped pot into a 200-BB pot. Kings and sixes with a nine kicker cannot justify automatic value escalation against repeated reraises. Stop raising and usually fold to the later reraises.

AJ raises and then calls a shove on 9h Ks 2h Jh 3d. Second pair is a bluff-catcher on a board where the heart flush completed on the turn. Prefer call or fold against the lead, and fold to the shove absent a strong exploitative read.

A6 offsuit calls a squeeze, calls a flop bet and raise on Td 2d 2s, then calls a turn shove on 9d against two opponents. It never makes a private pair or strong draw before committing. Prefer folding preflop or to the flop aggression; shared board pairs do not make this a strong made hand.
TT shoves over a river raise on 2s 4s 2h 3c Qc after already facing a turn raise. It is below queens, trips, overpairs and straights. Prefer folding to the river raise in the basic policy.

A9 check-raises on Qs 9d 2s Jh 7c and calls off. The nine is third pair on a connected board. Prefer folding or occasionally bluff-catching, rather than a default value check-raise; the later all-in call is cheap because of prior overinvestment.
Prefer calling a cheap river raise rather than relying on better hands folding to a reraise.
Treat raising top pair on a paired, three-flush board as model-sensitive and prefer calling.
Prefer calling with top pair on a connected river when the raising advantage depends on uncertain ranges.

J9s faces a three-bet at 40 BB effective, outside the 75–150 BB positional baseline. Keep advice provisional and exclude it from accuracy; do not use sample count as evidence of strategic correctness.
Keep an underpair to the ace as a showdown hand when raising is sensitive to range assumptions.
Recommend a supported moderate value raise instead of an enormous shove with two pair.
Prefer calling with an overpair when raising is sensitive to the concentration of flushes and other strong holdings.
Preserve a moderate two-pair value raise when it remains supported under stronger-made-hand ranges.
A9 offsuit facing a small-blind three-bet after opening the button is a fold in the simplified positional baseline. Raw equity and pot odds alone do not justify calling with a dominated offsuit hand.
Close preflop defense out of position: folding must remain accepted; raw equity alone does not establish a profitable call.
Close preflop defense in position against a small three-bet: preserve call/fold alternatives.
Top pair facing a river lead after two calls: accept calling and stress frequent normal-sized reraises.
Two pair facing three barrels: do not require a fragile raise-fold plan.
Rivered two pair: stress the large raise-fold size against frequent bot reraises; keep calling acceptable.

Reported hand 13: KK on 8c 3d 2h after a small BTN three-bet and two calls, checked to the preflop aggressor. A small value bet and checking are both reasonable; do not reject the half-pot bet category simply because both opponents rarely continue together. No actual opponent cards or future turn/river are retained.
